title: De lineis curvis non in eodem plano sitis, quae maximi minimive proprietate sunt praeditae

deep.reconstruction:
Problem: among space curves, find the one that makes ∫ w(v) ds extreme, where v = √(x²+y²+z²) is the distance from a fixed centre and ds = s dx with s = √(1+p²+q²), p = dy/dx, q = dz/dx. This is a geodesic (light-ray) problem for an isotropic, spherically symmetric 'refractive index' w(v).

On the previous page Euler derived the Euler–Lagrange system:
- (I) w′ s x dx/v = d(w/s)
- (II) w′ s y dx/v = d(wp/s)
- (III) w′ s z dx/v = d(wq/s)

Eliminating d(w/s) gave two equations:
- (y dx − x dy)/v² = w dp/(w′ v s²)
- (z dx − x dz)/v² = w dq/(w′ v s²)

On this page:
1. Dividing one equation by the other gives (z dx − x dz)/(y dx − x dy) = dq/dp. With dy = p dx and dz = q dx this becomes dq/(z − qx) = dp/(y − px).
2. Multiplying by −x, each numerator is the exact differential of its denominator, since d(z − qx) = −x dq and d(y − px) = −x dp. Logarithmic integration gives z − qx = m(y − px).
3. Back-substitution gives dq = m dp, hence q = mp + n, and then z = my + nx. The extremal therefore lies in a plane through the centre. This is the variational counterpart of the planarity of central-force orbits; in modern terms it expresses conservation of the 'angular momentum' r × (w T).
4. Eliminating z and q gives v² = x² + y² + (my + nx)² and s² = 1 + p² + (mp + n)².
5. Putting y = ux turns the remaining equation into −du/(1 + u² + (mu + n)²) = w dp/(w′ v (1 + p² + (mp + n)²)).
6. Writing r = w/(w′v), this becomes du/(1 + u² + (mu + n)²) + r dp/(1 + p² + (mp + n)²) = 0. Both terms have the same form and, as the next page shows, integrate to arctangents: angles measured inside the oblique plane, with γ² = m² + n² + 1.

The problem served is reducing the 3-D problem to a planar one in polar-type variables.
errors: The printed quotient on the right reads ∂y/∂p, which should be ∂q/∂p (printing error or q/y glyph confusion). Euler's next step uses ∂q/∂p correctly.
On the previous page, equation I is transcribed as w′sx∂x/s; it should be w′sx∂x/v. This is a transcription or print slip and does not affect the derivation.
All steps on this page are otherwise correct: d(z − qx) = −x dq, z − qx = m(y − px), q = mp + n, z = my + nx, and y dx − x dy = −x² du with v² = x²(1 + u² + (mu + n)²).

ideas.what: Extremals of ∫ w(r) ds (radially symmetric isotropic medium) lie in a plane through the centre, obtained by integrating the ratio of the transverse Euler–Lagrange equations.
ideas.modern_name: Planarity of motion under rotational symmetry / conservation of angular momentum (Noether); geodesics of a spherically symmetric conformal metric
ideas.usually_credited_to: Planarity of central-force orbits: Newton/Euler (Mechanica, 1736). Symmetry–conservation link: Jacobi, Noether (1918).
ideas.where_published: Planarity of central orbits appears in Euler's Mechanica (E15/E16). Similar isoperimetric and variational treatments appear in Methodus inveniendi (E65) for planar cases. A 3-D variational version elsewhere: unsure.

ideas.what: Reduction of the planar remaining equation via y = ux to two similar separable-looking differentials, each integrable as an arctangent (angles within the oblique plane).
ideas.modern_name: Polar-angle reduction in a tilted plane; Clairaut/Bouguer-type ray integral
ideas.where_published: Opera omnia I.25 (E740) likely; otherwise unsure

deep.surprise_reason: The page carries out a correct, routine reduction showing that extremals of a radially symmetric weighted-length functional are planar. The result is classical (central-force planarity / angular-momentum conservation), and nothing here seems to have gone unnoticed by the literature.
transcription_corrections: In the first displayed fraction, '= ∂y/∂p' should read '= ∂q/∂p' (the print has a q/y ambiguity; the mathematics requires q).
Previous page, equation I: 'w′sx∂x/s' should be 'w′sx∂x/v'.
